name: OMK 2A Heme — Summative 3 Objective Review · Board-Style Set 3 (Hard)

questions.stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 5 hours after she was found beside an open bottle of her mother's prenatal vitamins. She vomited four times and passed two bloody stools during the first 2 hours. For the past hour she has appeared well and has been playing in the waiting room. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes, cool extremities, and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Laboratory studies show:

    Arterial pH                 7.22
    PCO2                        26 mm Hg
    Serum bicarbonate           10 mEq/L
    Anion gap                   24 mEq/L
    Serum glucose               172 mg/dL
    Serum iron                  620 μg/dL (N=50–150)

An abdominal x-ray shows several radiopaque tablets in the stomach. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Activated charcoal, orally
B. Deferasirox, orally
C. Deferoxamine, intravenously
D. Dimercaprol, intramuscularly
E. Sodium bicarbonate, intravenously
questions.explanation: Free iron is a direct cellular toxin: it is corrosive to gastrointestinal mucosa (the early vomiting and bloody stools), it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation and drives anaerobic metabolism (the anion gap metabolic acidosis), and it causes vasodilation and third-spacing (the shock). Deferoxamine chelates FREE iron and is the antidote, given intravenously for a serum iron above roughly 500 μg/dL, shock, or significant acidosis — all three of which she has. Two traps are built in. The 'past hour she has appeared well' is the classic QUIESCENT PHASE at 6–24 hours, during which children look deceptively better while hepatic and cardiovascular injury progresses — but her blood pressure of 74/40 mm Hg shows she is not actually well. And the radiopaque tablets confirm ongoing absorption, which is why whole bowel irrigation is a reasonable adjunct for decontamination.

wrongExplanations.0: Activated charcoal does NOT adsorb iron — iron is a charged metal ion, not the organic molecule charcoal binds. Giving it here is useless and risks aspiration in a child who is already vomiting. This is the single most commonly tested fact about iron ingestion.
wrongExplanations.1: Deferasirox is an ORAL chelator used for CHRONIC iron overload, as in a repeatedly transfused thalassemic. It is not used in acute poisoning, and an oral agent is inappropriate in a vomiting child in shock.
wrongExplanations.3: Dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite) chelates arsenic, mercury, gold, and lead. It has no role in iron poisoning, and in some heavy-metal contexts chelator choice matters because the wrong agent can redistribute the metal.
wrongExplanations.4: Bicarbonate would treat the acidemia symptomatically while the iron that is generating it continues to be absorbed. The acidosis is a consequence, not the disease; removing the iron corrects it.

questions.eli5: Iron pills look like candy and a large dose is a poison, not a vitamin. She looked better for an hour, but that calm middle stage is a known trap — her blood pressure shows she is still very sick. A medicine given through the vein grabs the loose iron and carries it out in the urine.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has taken tamoxifen for 3 years following lumpectomy and radiation for an estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She comes to the office because of vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks. She has had no breast masses, bone pain, or weight loss. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F) and blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows blood in the vaginal vault and no adnexal masses. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an endometrial stripe of 14 mm. Endometrial biopsy shows complex hyperplasia with atypia. Which of the following best explains this complication?
choices: A. Aromatase inhibition increasing circulating estradiol concentrations
B. Complete estrogen receptor antagonism in all target tissues
C. Estrogen receptor agonist activity in endometrial tissue
D. Impaired CYP2D6-dependent conversion to the active metabolite
E. Upregulation of progesterone receptors within the myometrium
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a SELECTIVE estrogen receptor modulator, and the word selective is the whole answer: its effect depends on which coactivator and corepressor proteins are abundant in a given tissue. In BREAST tissue it recruits corepressors and behaves as an antagonist, which is the therapeutic effect. In ENDOMETRIUM it recruits coactivators and behaves as an AGONIST, driving proliferation → endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, and carcinoma. It is agonist in bone as well, which is why it preserves bone density, and it raises venous thromboembolism risk. Contrast the aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane), which block peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens and so have NO agonist activity anywhere: they cause osteoporosis and arthralgias instead of endometrial disease, are preferred in postmenopausal women, and are ineffective premenopausally because the ovary — not peripheral aromatase — is then the dominant estrogen source.

wrongExplanations.0: Tamoxifen does not inhibit aromatase; that is the mechanism of anastrozole and letrozole. Those drugs LOWER estrogen everywhere and therefore do not stimulate the endometrium at all.
wrongExplanations.1: If tamoxifen were a complete antagonist in every tissue it would protect the endometrium rather than stimulate it, and it would also cause bone loss. Its tissue-selective partial agonism is precisely what produces this complication.
wrongExplanations.3: This statement is TRUE — tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to endoxifen, which is why strong CYP2D6 inhibitors such as paroxetine can blunt its efficacy. But impaired activation would cause treatment FAILURE, not endometrial overstimulation, so it does not explain this finding.
wrongExplanations.4: Progesterone receptor upregulation is an estrogen-driven effect and is used as a marker of estrogen action, but it does not itself cause endometrial hyperplasia — and the myometrium is smooth muscle, not the endometrial lining that has become hyperplastic here.

questions.eli5: This drug is not a simple on-or-off switch — it blocks estrogen in breast tissue but imitates estrogen in the uterus. So the same pill that protects her breast is quietly stimulating her uterine lining. That is why any bleeding after menopause on this drug gets investigated.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the office for preconception counseling. She has a 12-year history of generalized epilepsy that has been well controlled on valproic acid for the past 4 years; she has had no seizures in that time. She hopes to conceive within the next 6 months. She eats a varied diet that includes fortified breakfast cereals and takes no other medications. She has never been pregnant. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding folic acid?
choices: A. Begin 0.4 mg daily at the time of the first positive pregnancy test
B. Begin 4 mg daily now, before conception
C. No supplementation is needed given her intake of fortified grains
D. Supplementation should be deferred until the second trimester to avoid masking vitamin B12 deficiency
E. Supplementation should be replaced by vitamin B12, which is the limiting cofactor
questions.explanation: Two variables decide this question, and both are pushed to the extreme by her valproate. TIMING: the neural tube closes by about day 28 after conception — often before a woman knows she is pregnant — so supplementation started at a positive pregnancy test is ALREADY TOO LATE for the defect it is meant to prevent. It must precede conception, ideally by at least 1 month. DOSE: the standard recommendation is 0.4 mg daily, but HIGH-RISK women take 4 mg daily — a previous neural-tube-defect pregnancy, pre-gestational diabetes, obesity, and antiepileptic drugs, valproate above all. Valproate both raises neural tube defect risk independently and interferes with folate metabolism. Folate is required for thymidylate synthesis and therefore for DNA replication, which is why the tissue that suffers is the one dividing fastest — the closing neural tube. (Separately, and beyond this question, valproate is the antiepileptic most associated with neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm, so whether to switch agents before conception is a genuine discussion to have with her neurologist.)

wrongExplanations.0: This is the right dose for an average-risk woman but at the WRONG time, and it is the trap. By the time a pregnancy test turns positive — typically 4 to 6 weeks' gestation — neural tube closure is complete or nearly so, and no amount of folate afterward can reverse it.
wrongExplanations.2: Grain fortification meaningfully reduced neural tube defects at a population level, but it delivers only about 0.1–0.2 mg daily. That is nowhere near sufficient for a woman on valproate, and dietary intake alone is not considered adequate even for average-risk women.
wrongExplanations.3: The concern that folate corrects the anemia of B12 deficiency while neurologic damage progresses is real — but it applies to an older patient being worked up for macrocytosis, not to a healthy 27-year-old planning a pregnancy. Deferring to the second trimester would miss the entire window in which folate acts.
wrongExplanations.4: Vitamin B12 is a genuine cofactor in the same one-carbon pathway, and deficiency does raise homocysteine — but the evidence for preventing neural tube defects rests specifically on FOLIC ACID, and she has no reason to be B12 deficient on a varied diet including animal products.

questions.eli5: The baby's spine and brain finish closing about four weeks after conception, which is usually before a pregnancy test turns positive. So the vitamin has to already be in her body before she conceives, not started once she finds out. Her seizure medicine also raises the risk, so she needs the high dose rather than the standard one.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the office because of a 5-month history of epigastric discomfort and early satiety. He has had no weight loss, vomiting, or melena. He takes no medications. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Upper endoscopy shows thickened, nodular gastric folds in the antrum without a discrete mass. Biopsy specimens show a dense monoclonal B-lymphocytic infiltrate of the lamina propria with lymphoepithelial lesions invading gastric glands. Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD20 and negative for CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1. Testing for Helicobacter pylori is positive, and fluorescence in situ hybridization for t(11;18) is NEGATIVE. Staging studies show disease confined to the stomach. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
choices: A. Combination chemotherapy with rituximab and an alkylating agent
B. Helicobacter pylori eradication with antibiotic therapy
C. Partial gastrectomy with regional lymph node dissection
D. Radiation therapy to the stomach and perigastric nodes
E. Splenectomy, as used in splenic marginal zone lymphoma
questions.explanation: This is extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach, and it is the cleanest illustration of why mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue matters. The normal stomach has essentially NO organized lymphoid tissue; chronic Helicobacter infection recruits it, and the resulting chronic antigenic stimulation drives a reactive B-cell population that eventually becomes a monoclonal neoplasm. Because the tumor initially remains ANTIGEN-DEPENDENT — it needs the continuing Helicobacter-driven T-cell help to survive — removing the antigen removes the growth signal, and roughly 70–80% of these lymphomas regress completely on antibiotics alone. That is an extraordinary fact: a cancer cured by treating an infection. The t(11;18) result is the load-bearing detail. That translocation creates an API2-MALT1 fusion that renders the clone antigen-INDEPENDENT, and those tumors do NOT regress with eradication and need lymphoma-directed therapy. His negative result predicts response, so eradication is the correct first move, with endoscopic surveillance to confirm regression.

wrongExplanations.0: Rituximab-based chemotherapy is the answer for disease that is t(11;18) POSITIVE, Helicobacter-negative, deeply invasive, disseminated beyond the stomach, or that fails to regress after successful eradication. Using it first here would treat with cytotoxic therapy a tumor that antibiotics alone will most likely cure.
wrongExplanations.2: Gastrectomy was historical management and is now reserved for complications such as perforation or uncontrollable hemorrhage. Removing the stomach to treat a lymphoma that responds to a 2-week antibiotic course is disproportionate.
wrongExplanations.3: Radiation is effective and is the standard salvage for localized disease that persists after eradication, or for a Helicobacter-negative tumor. It is second-line here precisely because eradication is likely to work.
wrongExplanations.4: Splenectomy is used in SPLENIC marginal zone lymphoma, a different member of the marginal zone family that presents with splenomegaly and cytopenias. His spleen is normal and his disease is confined to the stomach.

questions.eli5: The stomach does not normally contain immune tissue, but a chronic bacterial infection summons it there and keeps it switched on for years until it turns into a cancer. Because the cancer still depends on the bacteria to keep growing, killing the bacteria often makes the cancer disappear. One genetic change breaks that dependence — and he does not have it.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man undergoes excisional biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node that has persisted for 6 weeks following an illness characterized by fever, sore throat, and profound fatigue. A heterophile antibody test was positive at the time of that illness. He is otherwise well and takes no medications. Histologic examination of the node shows preserved overall architecture with markedly expanded, irregularly shaped follicles containing enlarged pale germinal centers with numerous mitotic figures and tingible-body macrophages, surrounded by a compressed mantle zone. Immunohistochemistry shows these centers are composed predominantly of CD20-positive cells. Which of the following processes is occurring within the expanded regions?
choices: A. Antigen-dependent B-cell maturation with somatic hypermutation and class switching
B. Antigen-independent B-cell maturation from pro-B cells to immature B cells
C. Antigen-independent rearrangement of T-cell receptor gene segments
D. Negative selection of autoreactive T lymphocytes against self-peptide
E. Positive selection of thymocytes capable of binding major histocompatibility complex
questions.explanation: Lymphocyte maturation splits cleanly into two phases, and the node tests whether you can place a structure in the right one. ANTIGEN-INDEPENDENT maturation happens in the primary lymphoid organs — B cells in the bone marrow, T cells in the thymus — and builds a diverse receptor repertoire before any antigen is ever seen. ANTIGEN-DEPENDENT maturation happens in the secondary lymphoid organs, including the lymph node, only after antigen arrives. Now locate the structure: GERMINAL CENTERS sit within FOLLICLES in the CORTEX and are B-cell territory, confirmed here by CD20 positivity. Inside them, antigen-activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation to refine antibody affinity and class-switch recombination to change isotype, with tingible-body macrophages clearing the many clones that fail selection. The rest of the node maps alongside this: the PARACORTEX is the T-cell zone (and is what expands most in a viral infection such as this one), and the MEDULLA holds antibody-secreting plasma cells and sinuses draining to the efferent lymphatic.

wrongExplanations.1: Pro-B to immature B maturation is antigen-INDEPENDENT and occurs in the BONE MARROW, not the lymph node. By the time a B cell reaches a germinal center it has long since completed that stage.
wrongExplanations.2: T-cell receptor gene rearrangement is also antigen-independent and occurs in the THYMUS. It would also be occurring in T cells, whereas these germinal center cells are CD20-positive B cells.
wrongExplanations.3: Negative selection deletes autoreactive lymphocytes and occurs in the thymic medulla for T cells (and in the marrow for B cells). It is a tolerance mechanism in a primary lymphoid organ, not an affinity-maturation process in a reactive node.
wrongExplanations.4: Positive selection of thymocytes on major histocompatibility complex occurs in the thymic CORTEX. The word cortex is the trap — a lymph node cortex and a thymic cortex are different tissues doing different jobs, and only the thymus contains thymocytes.

questions.eli5: Immune cells are built in the bone marrow and thymus before they ever meet a germ — that is the training phase. Once they meet a real germ, they gather in these round centers in the lymph node and fine-tune their antibodies to fit it better. The swelling in his neck is that fine-tuning happening at full speed.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-day history of fever, sore throat, myalgias, and a diffuse rash. He reports unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pharyngeal erythema without exudate, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, several shallow oral ulcers, and a nonpruritic maculopapular rash over the trunk. A heterophile antibody test is negative. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 3,200/mm3 with 42% lymphocytes and a platelet count of 118,000/mm3. A fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay is REACTIVE. A supplemental HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is NEGATIVE for antibodies to both HIV-1 and HIV-2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: A. HIV-1 Western blot
B. Measurement of the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count
C. Nucleic acid amplification testing for HIV-1 RNA
D. Repeat antigen/antibody immunoassay in 3 months
E. Testing for HLA-B*5701
questions.explanation: This is the discordant result the CDC algorithm is specifically designed to resolve, and it has one meaning. The fourth-generation assay detects BOTH p24 antigen and antibody; the supplemental assay detects ANTIBODY ONLY. A reactive screen with a negative differentiation assay therefore says: viral protein is present but antibodies have not yet developed — ACUTE HIV infection, inside the window period before seroconversion. The algorithm's third step is an HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid test, which will be strongly positive, often with a viral load in the millions. Getting this right is urgent for two reasons. Viral load peaks during acute infection, so this is when the patient is MOST infectious and onward transmission is most likely. And immediate antiretroviral therapy during acute infection limits the size of the latent reservoir. His clinical picture — the acute retroviral syndrome of fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, oral ulcers, and cytopenias with a NEGATIVE heterophile test — is mononucleosis-like, and mistaking it for Epstein-Barr virus is the standard clinical error.

wrongExplanations.0: The Western blot is obsolete in this algorithm and was removed precisely because it performs POORLY in acute infection — it detects antibody, so like the differentiation assay it would be negative or indeterminate here and would simply repeat the information already obtained.
wrongExplanations.1: The CD4 count stages established disease and determines the need for opportunistic infection prophylaxis. It does not confirm infection, and in acute infection it can fall transiently and mislead.
wrongExplanations.3: Waiting 3 months would eventually produce a positive antibody test, but it leaves a highly infectious patient undiagnosed and untreated through the exact period of peak transmissibility. The current algorithm exists so that no one has to wait.
wrongExplanations.4: HLA-B*5701 screening is performed before prescribing ABACAVIR, to avoid a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction. It is a treatment-selection test, not a diagnostic one, and it presumes the diagnosis is already established.

questions.eli5: The first test looks for both the virus's own protein and the body's antibodies against it; the second looks only for antibodies. A positive first test with a negative second one means the virus is there but his body has not made antibodies yet — a very new infection. A test that looks directly for the virus's genetic material settles it.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man is receiving intravenous alteplase for an acute ischemic stroke that began 90 minutes ago. Forty minutes into the infusion he develops a severe headache, vomits twice, and becomes progressively less responsive. His pulse is 58/min and blood pressure is 198/104 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows a new right hemiparesis and a dilating left pupil. The infusion is stopped. CT scan of the head without contrast shows a large left frontoparietal intraparenchymal hematoma with midline shift. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                              196,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            13 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       33 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  74 mg/dL (N=200–400)

In addition to neurosurgical consultation and blood pressure control, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
B. Fresh frozen plasma
C. Protamine sulfate
D. Tranexamic acid together with cryoprecipitate
E. Vitamin K
questions.explanation: Fibrinolytics convert plasminogen to PLASMIN, which digests fibrin — and also circulating fibrinogen, which is why his fibrinogen has fallen to 74 mg/dL while his PT and aPTT remain normal. That isolated pattern is the fingerprint of a lytic state and tells you what to replace. Reversal mirrors the drug in two moves: give CRYOPRECIPITATE to restore fibrinogen (target above roughly 150 mg/dL), since it is the concentrated fibrinogen product and plasma cannot deliver enough in a tolerable volume; and give an ANTIFIBRINOLYTIC — tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid — which blocks the lysine binding sites plasminogen uses to dock onto fibrin, stopping further plasmin generation. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage is the feared complication of thrombolysis, which is why the contraindications all describe places a dissolved clot would be catastrophic: prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3 months, intracranial neoplasm or vascular malformation, suspected aortic dissection, active internal bleeding, significant closed head trauma within 3 months, and severe uncontrolled hypertension.

wrongExplanations.0: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate replaces the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X and is the answer for urgent WARFARIN reversal. It contains essentially no fibrinogen, which is the one thing this patient has lost, and his PT is normal.
wrongExplanations.1: Fresh frozen plasma contains fibrinogen only at physiologic concentration, so restoring a level of 74 mg/dL would require a volume this patient cannot safely receive — the same ocean-and-teacup problem as in any severe hypofibrinogenemia. It also does nothing to stop ongoing plasmin activity.
wrongExplanations.2: Protamine sulfate is the antidote for UNFRACTIONATED HEPARIN, binding it in a stable salt (with partial activity against low-molecular-weight heparin). His aPTT is normal and he has received no heparin.
wrongExplanations.4: Vitamin K restores gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors over 6 to 24 hours and reverses WARFARIN, not a fibrinolytic. Both the mechanism and the timescale are wrong for a patient herniating now.

questions.eli5: The clot-busting drug works by switching on an enzyme that chews up the mesh of clots — including the raw material his blood needs to clot anywhere else. So he is given back that raw material in concentrated form, plus a second drug that switches the chewing enzyme off. Two moves that exactly undo what the first drug did.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma achieved a complete metabolic remission after six cycles of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. Fourteen months later she has recurrent adenopathy and drenching night sweats. Biopsy of an axillary node confirms recurrent lymphoma, and molecular studies show the same clonal immunoglobulin heavy chain rearrangement as her original tumor. Compared with the original specimen, the recurrent tumor shows markedly increased expression of P-glycoprotein encoded by MDR1. Retreatment with the same regimen produces no response. Which of the following best explains this tumor's resistance?
choices: A. Amplification of the dihydrofolate reductase gene
B. Enhanced repair of alkylated DNA by O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase
C. Increased adenosine triphosphate-dependent efflux of drug from the tumor cell
D. Loss of the reduced folate carrier required for drug uptake
E. Point mutation of topoisomerase II reducing drug binding affinity
questions.explanation: P-glycoprotein is an adenosine triphosphate-driven efflux PUMP in the cell membrane. Overexpressing it means the tumor cell exports drug faster than it accumulates, so the intracellular concentration never reaches a lethal level. Its clinical importance is its BREADTH: it handles a wide range of large, hydrophobic natural-product drugs — anthracyclines such as doxorubicin, vinca alkaloids such as vincristine, taxanes, and etoposide — so a single change confers MULTIDRUG resistance across several classes at once. This is why the underlying chemotherapeutic principles matter: combine drugs with DIFFERENT mechanisms and NON-OVERLAPPING toxicities, give them at maximum tolerated dose intensity on schedule, and treat early, because resistant subclones arise spontaneously in proportion to tumor size and to the number of divisions the tumor has undergone. Note also that her relapse is the SAME clone rather than a new one, which is what makes acquired resistance rather than a second primary the explanation.

wrongExplanations.0: Dihydrofolate reductase amplification is a resistance mechanism to METHOTREXATE — the cell simply makes more of the target enzyme than the drug can inhibit. Methotrexate is not in this regimen, and this mechanism is drug-specific rather than multidrug.
wrongExplanations.1: O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase removes alkyl adducts from guanine and confers resistance to ALKYLATING agents, most famously temozolomide in glioma (where MGMT promoter methylation predicts response). It would not explain failure of vincristine or doxorubicin.
wrongExplanations.3: Loss of the reduced folate carrier blocks drug UPTAKE and is another methotrexate-specific mechanism. Note that it is the mirror image of the correct answer — failure to get in rather than being pumped out — which makes it the most tempting distractor.
wrongExplanations.4: A topoisomerase II point mutation is a genuine mechanism of resistance to doxorubicin and etoposide, but it is target-specific: it would not protect the cell from vincristine, which acts on microtubules. It also would not explain the P-glycoprotein finding that the question hands you.

questions.eli5: Her cancer cells have installed pumps in their outer membrane that throw the drugs back out before they can work. Because those pumps grab several different drugs, one change made the tumor resistant to most of her regimen at once. That is why chemotherapy uses several drugs with different mechanisms from the very start.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department in late July because of a 5-day history of fever, chills, drenching sweats, and dark urine. He underwent splenectomy 20 years ago after a motor vehicle collision. He lives on Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, gardens daily, and has not traveled outside the United States. He recalls no tick bite. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  7.4 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  22%
    Platelet count              68,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count          6.8%
    Lactate dehydrogenase       880 U/L
    Total bilirubin             4.2 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.5 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)

A Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear shows small intraerythrocytic ring forms, occasional tetrads arranged in a cross, and extracellular forms; no crescent-shaped forms and no intracellular brown pigment are seen. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
choices: A. Anaplasma phagocytophilum
B. Babesia microti
C. Ehrlichia chaffeensis
D. Plasmodium falciparum
E. Plasmodium vivax
questions.explanation: Four findings converge. GEOGRAPHY: Nantucket is the endemic focus for which Babesia microti is named in the literature, transmitted by Ixodes scapularis — the same tick as Lyme disease — with no foreign travel to suggest malaria. MORPHOLOGY: the tetrad of merozoites arranged in a cross (the Maltese cross) is essentially pathognomonic, and equally important are the two NEGATIVES — Babesia produces no hemozoin pigment because it does not digest hemoglobin the way Plasmodium does, and it forms no gametocytes, so the banana-shaped crescents of falciparum are absent. Extracellular forms are also characteristic. HOST: asplenia is the single greatest risk factor for severe, high-parasitemia babesiosis, because the spleen clears parasitized erythrocytes. And the LABORATORY picture is intravascular hemolysis — high lactate dehydrogenase, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, undetectable haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, hemoglobinuria. Treatment is atovaquone plus azithromycin, or clindamycin plus quinine in severe disease, with exchange transfusion for very high parasitemia.

wrongExplanations.0: Anaplasma phagocytophilum shares the Ixodes vector and the same geography, so coinfection is common and it is the strongest epidemiologic competitor. It is excluded by cell type: it forms morulae inside GRANULOCYTES, not inside erythrocytes, and it causes leukopenia with transaminase elevation rather than a brisk hemolytic anemia.
wrongExplanations.2: Ehrlichia chaffeensis is transmitted by the Lone Star tick in the southeastern and south-central United States and forms morulae within MONOCYTES. Both the vector distribution and the infected cell are wrong.
wrongExplanations.3: Plasmodium falciparum is the closest morphologic mimic — it also produces small ring forms and high parasitemia — but it requires travel to an endemic area, produces banana-shaped GAMETOCYTES, and deposits brown hemozoin PIGMENT. The stem explicitly excludes both, and falciparum does not form tetrads or extracellular forms.
wrongExplanations.4: Plasmodium vivax also requires travel exposure, and its morphology is distinctive in the opposite direction: it enlarges the infected erythrocyte, produces Schuffner stippling, and shows ameboid trophozoites rather than small rings and tetrads.

questions.eli5: A tick on Nantucket passed him a parasite that lives inside red blood cells and bursts them open. Under the microscope four of the parasites sometimes sit in a cross shape, which is the giveaway. He has no spleen, and the spleen is the organ that would normally filter these infected cells out — so his infection got severe fast.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV infection comes to the office because of skin lesions that have appeared over the past 6 weeks and now bleed with minor trauma. He stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago. He adopted two stray kittens 3 months ago and has several healed scratches on his forearms. He has had fevers and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows more than 20 friable, dome-shaped, red-to-violaceous papulonodules ranging from 4 to 20 mm over the trunk and extremities, several with collarettes of scale; the oral mucosa is clear. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 42/μL. Biopsy of a lesion shows a lobular proliferation of plump capillaries lined by protuberant endothelial cells, with a neutrophilic infiltrate and amphophilic granular material; Warthin-Starry silver staining shows clumps of small bacilli. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Antiretroviral therapy alone, without antimicrobial therapy
B. Doxycycline or erythromycin
C. Intralesional vinblastine
D. Liposomal doxorubicin
E. Radiation therapy to the involved skin
F. Surgical excision of all lesions
questions.explanation: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella henselae (cat and kitten exposure, as here) or Bartonella quintana (body louse exposure), and it occurs almost exclusively at CD4 counts below about 100/μL. The organism induces vascular proliferation through hypoxia-inducible-factor-driven vascular endothelial growth factor signalling — a bacterium literally making the host grow blood vessels. Everything in this biopsy is the discriminator against KAPOSI SARCOMA, which looks nearly identical to the naked eye: bacillary angiomatosis shows PLUMP epithelioid endothelium, a NEUTROPHILIC infiltrate, and visible bacilli on Warthin-Starry silver stain, whereas Kaposi sarcoma shows SPINDLE cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin, a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, no organisms, and positive HHV-8 (LANA-1) immunostaining. The distinction is worth making precisely: this one is CURABLE WITH ANTIBIOTICS — erythromycin or doxycycline for at least 3 months — and untreated it disseminates to liver and spleen as peliosis hepatis and can be fatal. Antiretroviral therapy should be restarted alongside, with attention to immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

wrongExplanations.0: Restarting antiretroviral therapy is essential and will raise his CD4 count over months, but it does not treat the established infection. Bacillary angiomatosis is a bacterial disease that disseminates to liver and spleen as peliosis hepatis and can be fatal, so antimicrobial therapy cannot be deferred while immune reconstitution is awaited.
wrongExplanations.2: Intralesional vinblastine is a local treatment for limited KAPOSI SARCOMA. It would be chemotherapy given for a bacterial infection, and it would not prevent dissemination to the liver and spleen.
wrongExplanations.3: Liposomal doxorubicin is first-line systemic therapy for extensive or visceral KAPOSI SARCOMA. The neutrophilic infiltrate and silver-positive bacilli here point to infection rather than to an HHV-8-driven vascular tumor.
wrongExplanations.4: Radiation is used palliatively for bulky or symptomatic Kaposi lesions. It has no role against an organism that is disseminating haematogenously, and it would irradiate more than 20 separate sites.
wrongExplanations.5: Excision might be considered for a single isolated lesion, but he has more than 20 and a systemic febrile illness with weight loss, which indicates disseminated infection requiring systemic antibiotics.

questions.eli5: His new kittens carried a bacterium that makes the body sprout clumps of tiny blood vessels, which look like purple bleeding bumps on the skin. They look almost exactly like a cancer that people with advanced HIV also get. A silver stain showed actual bacteria inside — so antibiotics cure it.

questions.stem:
A 2-month-old boy born at 39 weeks' gestation is brought to the office for a routine health maintenance visit. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated and he required no resuscitation. He breastfeeds vigorously every 3 hours, has 6 wet diapers daily, and has gained 1.4 kg since birth, tracking along the 50th percentile. He has had no jaundice, bleeding, or infection. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 132/min, and respirations are 38/min. Physical examination shows a well-appearing infant with no pallor, no organomegaly, and no murmur. A complete blood count obtained as part of a research protocol shows:

    Hemoglobin                  9.4 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  28%
    Mean corpuscular volume     92 μm3
    Reticulocyte count          1.2%
    Leukocyte count             9,800/mm3
    Platelet count              340,000/mm3

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Hemoglobin electrophoresis
B. Measurement of the serum ferritin concentration
C. No further evaluation or treatment
D. Oral ferrous sulfate therapy
E. Transfusion of packed erythrocytes
questions.explanation: This is the PHYSIOLOGIC NADIR OF INFANCY, and recognizing it depends entirely on knowing that reference ranges are age-specific. In utero the fetus lives at low oxygen tension, so erythropoietin is high and the newborn arrives polycythemic with a hemoglobin around 16–18 g/dL. At birth arterial oxygen saturation jumps from roughly 50% to 95%, erythropoietin production shuts off almost completely, and erythropoiesis nearly stops. Meanwhile the high-hemoglobin newborn cells — which are largely fetal hemoglobin with a shortened lifespan of about 70–90 days — are steadily removed. The hemoglobin therefore falls to a nadir of about 9–11 g/dL at 8 to 12 weeks in a term infant, at which point tissue oxygen delivery finally falls enough to restart erythropoietin and the count recovers on its own. Every feature here confirms the physiologic process: he is thriving, well perfused, normocytic, and the low reticulocyte count is APPROPRIATE rather than alarming, because the marrow is correctly switched off. Treating this would be treating a normal developmental value.

wrongExplanations.0: Hemoglobin electrophoresis would be the answer for suspected thalassemia or a sickling disorder — which would require microcytosis, a family history, or a positive newborn screen. It is also difficult to interpret at this age, because fetal hemoglobin still predominates and the switch to adult hemoglobin is incomplete until around 6 months.
wrongExplanations.1: Ferritin measurement presupposes iron deficiency, which does not occur in a term breastfed infant at 2 months. Maternal iron transferred in the third trimester supplies a term infant for roughly the first 6 months, which is why iron deficiency is a problem of the second half of infancy — and of PRETERM infants, who miss that transfer and reach a deeper, earlier nadir.
wrongExplanations.3: Oral iron would be the answer at 9 to 12 months in an infant with a MICROCYTIC anemia and low ferritin. His mean corpuscular volume of 92 μm3 is normal for age, and iron is not the limiting factor when the marrow has deliberately stopped producing.
wrongExplanations.4: Transfusion would be the answer for a symptomatic infant — poor feeding, tachypnea at rest, failure to gain weight, or hemodynamic compromise. He is thriving on the 50th percentile with normal perfusion, and transfusing would suppress his own recovering erythropoiesis while exposing him to donor risk.

questions.eli5: Before birth a baby lives in a low-oxygen environment and makes lots of red blood cells. After the first breath there is far more oxygen available, so the body switches red cell production off for a couple of months and the count naturally drifts down. It bottoms out around now and then climbs back up by itself.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of fatigue and intermittent diarrhea. She has lost 7 kg (15 lb) over the past year without dieting. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor, angular cheilitis, and a smooth tongue. Sensation to vibration is decreased over both great toes. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                      9.6 g/dL
    Hematocrit                      29%
    Mean corpuscular volume         88 μm3
    Red cell distribution width     21.4% (N=11.5–14.5)
    Reticulocyte count              0.7%
    Serum ferritin                  7 ng/mL
    Serum vitamin B12               138 pg/mL (N=200–900)
    Methylmalonic acid              Increased
    Tissue transglutaminase IgA     Increased

A peripheral blood smear shows a dimorphic population of small hypochromic erythrocytes together with oval macrocytes, and occasional neutrophils with six nuclear lobes. Which of the following best explains this patient's normal mean corpuscular volume?
choices: A. Anemia of inflammation superimposed on untreated celiac disease
B. Coexisting alpha thalassemia trait offsetting the macrocytosis of B12 deficiency
C. Reticulocytosis from a marrow response raising the measured mean cell volume
D. Simultaneous iron and vitamin B12 deficiency with opposing effects on cell size
E. Spurious measurement caused by cold agglutinins clumping erythrocytes
questions.explanation: The mean corpuscular volume is a MEAN, and a mean can be normal because nothing is wrong or because two opposite abnormalities cancel. Two findings expose which it is here. The red cell distribution width is 21.4% — a measure of how much cell SIZE VARIES, and it is markedly increased, meaning the population is wildly heterogeneous rather than uniformly normal. And the smear is explicitly DIMORPHIC: small hypochromic cells sitting alongside oval macrocytes, with hypersegmented neutrophils. She has celiac disease damaging the proximal small bowel, where IRON is absorbed, and extensive disease also impairs terminal ileal B12 absorption — confirmed by a ferritin of 7 ng/mL and a low B12 with an elevated methylmalonic acid. Two deficiencies, one microcytic and one macrocytic, averaging to 88 μm3. This is why the rule is to read the mean corpuscular volume FIRST but never alone: check the distribution width and look at the smear, because a normal mean can be two diseases hiding each other. Replace both — and if only folate or only iron were given, the neurologic damage from B12 deficiency would continue to progress.

wrongExplanations.0: Anemia of inflammation is typically normocytic and could in principle contribute, but it is excluded by the ferritin. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and RISES with inflammation; a value of 7 ng/mL is unequivocal iron deficiency and cannot be explained by an inflammatory block.
wrongExplanations.1: Thalassemia trait would indeed pull the mean volume down, and it is the most tempting alternative. But it produces a NORMAL red cell distribution width, because every cell is uniformly small, and it does not cause a low ferritin — her ferritin of 7 ng/mL proves true iron deficiency, and her celiac disease supplies the mechanism for both deficits.
wrongExplanations.2: Reticulocytes are larger than mature erythrocytes and can raise the mean volume slightly, but only when they are numerous. Her reticulocyte count is 0.7%, which is low — the marrow lacks the raw materials to respond at all.
wrongExplanations.4: Cold agglutinins clump erythrocytes so the analyzer counts each clump as one large cell, giving a falsely HIGH mean volume, a falsely low erythrocyte count, and a mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration above 37 g/dL. The tell-tale mismatch between hemoglobin and hematocrit is absent here — 29% is almost exactly three times 9.6 g/dL.

questions.eli5: Average cell size looked normal, but that is because she has two problems pulling in opposite directions — some cells are too small and some too big, and they average out. The clue is a number showing how much the sizes vary, which was very high. Looking at the actual slide showed both populations side by side.

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman comes to the office in January because of a 3-month history of fatigue and of painful bluish discoloration of her fingers, nose, and ears whenever she goes outdoors, which resolves indoors. She was treated for an atypical pneumonia 4 months ago. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, and dusky discoloration of the fingertips and earlobes that resolves with warming. There is no splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  27%
    Reticulocyte count          7.6%
    Total bilirubin             3.0 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.4 mg/dL
    Lactate dehydrogenase       498 U/L
    Haptoglobin                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)

A direct antiglobulin test is POSITIVE for complement C3d and NEGATIVE for IgG. The cold agglutinin titer is markedly increased. A peripheral blood smear prepared at room temperature shows clumping of erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
choices: A. Avoidance of cold exposure
B. Intravenous immune globulin
C. Prednisone
D. Rituximab
E. Splenectomy
questions.explanation: The direct antiglobulin pattern names the disease and dictates the treatment. C3d POSITIVE with IgG NEGATIVE means a COLD agglutinin — an IgM autoantibody that binds erythrocytes in the cooled peripheral circulation, fixes complement there, then falls off as the cell returns to the warm core, leaving only C3d behind. Two consequences follow directly. First, the acrocyanosis: IgM is pentameric and agglutinates cells in cold acral vessels, producing the reversible dusky fingers, nose, and ears. Second, and this is the treatment point, the complement-coated cells are cleared by KUPFFER CELLS IN THE LIVER, not by splenic macrophages — which is exactly why the therapies that work in WARM (IgG-mediated) autoimmune hemolysis fail here. Her preceding atypical pneumonia points to Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a classic secondary trigger, and post-infectious cold agglutinin disease is usually self-limited. So first-line management is thermal avoidance, keeping the patient and any infused fluids warm, and treating the underlying cause.

wrongExplanations.1: Intravenous immune globulin saturates Fc receptors on splenic macrophages and helps in IgG-mediated destruction, particularly immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Destruction here is complement-mediated and hepatic, so blockading splenic Fc receptors accomplishes little.
wrongExplanations.2: Prednisone is first-line for WARM autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where the antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and the spleen removes antibody-coated cells. It is characteristically INEFFECTIVE in cold agglutinin disease — reaching for it here is the error this item is built around.
wrongExplanations.3: Rituximab depletes the CD20-positive B-cell clone producing the IgM and is genuinely effective — but it is reserved for severe, symptomatic, or transfusion-dependent primary cold agglutinin disease. In post-infectious secondary disease expected to resolve on its own, it is not the initial step.
wrongExplanations.4: Splenectomy removes the site of IgG-mediated extravascular destruction and helps in warm autoimmune hemolysis and hereditary spherocytosis. It is of little value in cold agglutinin disease because the liver, not the spleen, is doing the clearing — and she has no splenomegaly.

questions.eli5: Her antibody only grabs red cells where the blood is coolest — fingers, nose, ears — which is why those turn blue outdoors and recover indoors. The damaged cells are then destroyed in the liver rather than the spleen. So keeping warm is the treatment, and the usual drugs that work on spleen-based destruction do not help here.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman received 2 units of packed red blood cells 8 days ago for postpartum hemorrhage. The transfusion was uneventful, and her hemoglobin concentration rose appropriately to 10.2 g/dL. She now comes to the office because of fatigue and yellowing of her eyes for 2 days. She has had no vaginal bleeding since discharge, no fever, and no dark urine. She has had three prior pregnancies. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 94/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and pallor; the uterus is well involuted and there is no abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  7.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  24%
    Reticulocyte count          5.4%
    Total bilirubin             3.2 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.4 mg/dL
    Lactate dehydrogenase       460 U/L
    Haptoglobin                 14 mg/dL (N=30–200)

A direct antiglobulin test is positive. Antibody screening, which was negative before the transfusion, now identifies an anti-Jk-a (Kidd) alloantibody. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
choices: A. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia arising independently of the recent transfusion episode
B. Bacterial contamination of the transfused units during collection
C. Hemolysis caused by ABO incompatibility between donor and recipient
D. Re-exposure to a minor erythrocyte antigen triggering a memory antibody response
E. Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease from non-irradiated cells
questions.explanation: This is a DELAYED hemolytic transfusion reaction, and the timing is the whole diagnosis. She was sensitized to the Kidd antigen during a previous pregnancy, when fetal cells carrying paternal antigens entered her circulation. Over the following years the antibody titer fell BELOW THE DETECTION THRESHOLD of the pretransfusion screen — which is why that screen was negative and the units were correctly issued as compatible. Re-exposure to Jk-a-positive donor cells then triggered a memory (anamnestic) response, and the titer climbed over roughly a week until it was high enough to coat and destroy the transfused cells. The result is exactly what is seen: a hemoglobin that rose appropriately and then fell 5 to 10 days later WITHOUT bleeding, with extravascular hemolysis — unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, a positive antiglobulin test — and a newly detectable alloantibody. Kidd antibodies are notorious for precisely this behavior because they evanesce so reliably, which is why a permanent antibody record must follow the patient for all future transfusions.

wrongExplanations.0: An autoantibody would react with her OWN erythrocytes and would not appear as a specific alloantibody against a single donor antigen 8 days after a transfusion. The identification of anti-Jk-a, plus the temporal relationship, points to alloimmunization.
wrongExplanations.1: Bacterial contamination causes a SEPTIC transfusion reaction — high fever, rigors, and rapid circulatory collapse DURING or shortly after the transfusion, classically with a room-temperature platelet unit. She was well for 8 days and has no fever.
wrongExplanations.2: ABO incompatibility causes an ACUTE hemolytic reaction within minutes: back and flank pain, hypotension, pink plasma, and hemoglobinuria from INTRAVASCULAR complement-mediated lysis. Her reaction is delayed, extravascular, and she has no hemoglobinuria — and it involves a minor antigen, not ABO.
wrongExplanations.4: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease appears 1 to 6 weeks later with PANCYTOPENIA, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction, is usually fatal, and is prevented by irradiating the product. She has an isolated hemolytic anemia with a healthy reticulocyte response, not marrow failure.

questions.eli5: During an earlier pregnancy she quietly built an antibody against a blood marker she does not carry herself. Over the years it faded to a level too low for the lab to detect, so the donated blood tested as a match. The new blood woke that memory up, and about a week later the antibody destroyed the transfused cells.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of extensive spontaneous bruising and a large, painful swelling of the right thigh that developed over 3 days without trauma. He has never had abnormal bleeding, including after an appendectomy at age 24 and two dental extractions in his fifties. There is no family history of a bleeding disorder. He takes no anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs, or herbal supplements. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tense, tender right thigh with overlying ecchymosis, and scattered large ecchymoses over the trunk. There is no joint swelling and no petechiae. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                              244,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       68 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  340 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    Factor VIII activity                        4% (N=50–150)

A 1:1 mixing study with normal plasma performed IMMEDIATELY corrects the activated partial thromboplastin time to 34 seconds. After incubation of the same mixture for 2 hours at 37°C, the activated partial thromboplastin time is 64 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
B. Autoantibody directed against factor VIII
C. Factor XII deficiency
D. Mild hemophilia A, previously undiagnosed
E. Von Willebrand disease, type 3
questions.explanation: The incubated mixing study is the entire question, and it exists to catch exactly this diagnosis. A simple factor DEFICIENCY corrects on mixing and STAYS corrected, because normal plasma supplies the missing factor. A classical inhibitor such as a lupus anticoagulant fails to correct IMMEDIATELY, because it interferes with the assay at once. Autoantibodies against factor VIII are different: they are TIME- AND TEMPERATURE-DEPENDENT, binding factor VIII progressively rather than instantaneously. So the immediate mix looks corrected — enough factor VIII is briefly present — and after 30 to 120 minutes at 37°C the antibody has neutralized the added factor VIII and the clotting time drifts back out. That biphasic pattern is essentially diagnostic of acquired hemophilia A. The clinical picture fits: an ELDERLY patient with NO personal or family bleeding history who suddenly develops severe soft tissue and muscle bleeding, a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and platelet count, and a very low factor VIII. It is often associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease, or the postpartum state. Management is bypassing agents (recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate) for the bleeding, plus immunosuppression to eradicate the antibody — NOT factor VIII concentrate, which the inhibitor will neutralize.

wrongExplanations.0: Antiphospholipid antibodies fail to correct on the IMMEDIATE mix, because they act on the phospholipid in the reagent instantly, and they correct with added excess phospholipid. They also cause THROMBOSIS rather than bleeding — this patient is bleeding severely.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT and causes no bleeding at all, which is the opposite of this presentation. Being a deficiency, it would also correct on mixing and stay corrected, and it would not depress factor VIII activity.
wrongExplanations.3: Congenital mild hemophilia A would give the same low factor VIII, but it is X-linked and lifelong — it would not spare him through an appendectomy and two dental extractions and then appear at 72. Critically, it is a deficiency, so BOTH the immediate and the incubated mix would correct.
wrongExplanations.4: Type 3 von Willebrand disease causes a secondary reduction in factor VIII, since von Willebrand factor is its carrier protein. But it is severe, recessive, and presents in childhood with mucocutaneous bleeding, von Willebrand antigen would be nearly absent, and mixing would correct.

questions.eli5: Mixing his blood with normal blood fixed the test right away, which normally means he was simply missing an ingredient. But leaving the mixture warm for two hours undid the fix — something in his plasma was slowly destroying the ingredient that had just been added. That slow-acting antibody is the diagnosis, and it is why the test has to be run twice.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a history of two unprovoked deep venous thromboses and one ischemic stroke, and three consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses. Testing on two occasions 12 weeks apart has shown a lupus anticoagulant, an anticardiolipin IgG antibody, and an anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG antibody, all persistently positive. She has been maintained on rivaroxaban for 14 months. She now comes to the emergency department because of sudden right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia. She reports taking every dose. Her blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. MRI of the brain shows an acute left middle cerebral artery territory infarct. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 108,000/mm3, a normal prothrombin time, and no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in her long-term anticoagulation?
choices: A. Add hydroxychloroquine to the current rivaroxaban regimen
B. Add low-dose aspirin to the current rivaroxaban regimen
C. Increase the rivaroxaban dose and continue current monitoring
D. Switch to apixaban, another direct oral factor Xa inhibitor, at full dose
E. Switch to warfarin, targeting an international normalized ratio of 2 to 3
questions.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important carve-out on the list of situations where a direct oral anticoagulant must NOT be used, and it is the one where the evidence shows actual HARM rather than merely absent benefit. Randomized trials comparing rivaroxaban with warfarin in TRIPLE-POSITIVE patients — lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, exactly this patient — were stopped early for an excess of ARTERIAL thrombotic events, including stroke, in the rivaroxaban arm. Her arterial stroke while fully adherent is that failure happening. The correct management is a vitamin K antagonist with an international normalized ratio target of 2 to 3, continued indefinitely, because her syndrome is a persistent risk factor and her events are unprovoked. Note two supporting details in the stem: she meets the formal diagnostic requirement of persistence on testing 12 weeks apart PLUS a clinical criterion, and the mild thrombocytopenia is characteristic — the lupus anticoagulant is misnamed twice over, since most patients do not have lupus and it prolongs clotting in vitro while causing thrombosis in vivo.

wrongExplanations.1: Adding aspirin to a failing anticoagulant addresses the platelet limb while leaving in place the drug that has been shown to underperform in this syndrome. Antiplatelet therapy has a role in primary prevention in some antibody-positive patients, but it does not substitute for switching off a harmful agent.
wrongExplanations.0: Hydroxychloroquine has antithrombotic and immunomodulatory properties and is often used adjunctively, especially in antiphospholipid syndrome associated with lupus. It is an adjunct, not a correction of the central error of remaining on a direct oral anticoagulant.
wrongExplanations.2: Increasing the dose treats this as underdosing. The problem is not the amount of drug but the class: the failures occurred at standard therapeutic doses, and higher doses would add bleeding risk without addressing the mechanism.
wrongExplanations.3: Switching to another agent within the SAME class is the most tempting wrong answer. Apixaban has attractive properties elsewhere — oral loading without a heparin lead-in, usability in renal impairment, possibly the lowest bleeding risk of the four — but the antiphospholipid carve-out applies to direct oral anticoagulants as a class, and apixaban has likewise underperformed here.

questions.eli5: Her antibodies cause clots, and the newer once-daily blood thinners have been shown in trials to work poorly for this specific condition — patients on them had more strokes. She had a stroke while taking every dose, which is that failure. The older drug with regular blood monitoring is the one proven to work here.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry is admitted for treatment of newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma. His leukocyte count is 96,000/mm3, lactate dehydrogenase is 4,200 U/L, and uric acid is 12.8 mg/dL, and CT shows bulky retroperitoneal adenopathy. He is given intravenous fluids and a single dose of rasburicase before the first cycle of chemotherapy. Six hours later he becomes dyspneic and appears dusky. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 124/min, and respirations are 28/min. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 84% that does not improve with 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask, although the arterial partial pressure of oxygen on that mask is 340 mm Hg. Blood drawn for testing appears chocolate brown and does not redden on exposure to air. Hemoglobin has fallen from 11.4 to 7.9 g/dL, and a peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes with peripheral membrane defects and irregular inclusions. Which of the following should have been assessed before administering this drug?
choices: A. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity
B. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity
C. Haptoglobin concentration
D. Serum methemoglobin concentration
E. Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
F. Uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 genotype
questions.explanation: Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts uric acid to allantoin — and the reaction generates HYDROGEN PEROXIDE as a stoichiometric byproduct. A normal erythrocyte disposes of that peroxide using glutathione, which must be continuously regenerated by NADPH from the hexose monophosphate shunt, whose rate-limiting enzyme is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. In a G6PD-deficient patient the NADPH supply fails, peroxide accumulates, and two things happen simultaneously: hemoglobin is oxidized to METHEMOGLOBIN, and denatured hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies that splenic macrophages pluck out, leaving the bite cells described here. That explains the otherwise paradoxical picture — profound cyanosis with a saturation of 84% that will not correct on 100% oxygen despite an arterial oxygen tension of 340 mm Hg, because the problem is that the hemoglobin cannot CARRY oxygen, not that the lungs cannot deliver it — plus chocolate-brown blood and an acute drop in hemoglobin. Rasburicase is therefore CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency, and screening is mandatory before use in patients of African, Mediterranean, or Southeast Asian ancestry. Methylene blue is also contraindicated as a treatment here, because its own reduction requires NADPH.

wrongExplanations.0: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity is measured before FLUOROURACIL or capecitabine, where deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal mucositis and myelosuppression. It is a real pretreatment pharmacogenomic screen attached to the wrong drug class.
wrongExplanations.2: Haptoglobin would be consumed during this hemolysis and is a useful confirmatory marker AFTER the fact. It is not a pretreatment screening test and would not have identified the vulnerability that made this drug dangerous.
wrongExplanations.3: A methemoglobin level is the test that CONFIRMS what is happening now and should certainly be sent. But the question asks what should have been checked BEFOREHAND — a baseline methemoglobin in a healthy young man would have been normal and would have predicted nothing.
wrongExplanations.4: Thiopurine methyltransferase activity is measured before AZATHIOPRINE or 6-mercaptopurine, where deficiency causes life-threatening myelosuppression. It is a genuine and commonly tested pharmacogenomic screen, but it is the wrong drug — a well-constructed distractor for exactly that reason.
wrongExplanations.5: UGT1A1 genotyping is performed before IRINOTECAN, where reduced-function alleles predict severe neutropenia and diarrhea. Again a real pharmacogenomic test attached to the wrong agent.

questions.eli5: The drug that lowers uric acid makes hydrogen peroxide as a waste product, and red blood cells need a particular enzyme to mop that up. He inherited a shortage of that enzyme, so the peroxide wrecked his hemoglobin — turning it into a form that cannot carry oxygen, which is why his blood is brown and oxygen does not help. A simple blood test beforehand would have flagged it.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase has taken imatinib for 3 years. His BCR-ABL1 transcript level fell steadily during the first 18 months to 0.05% on the international scale. Over the past 6 months the transcript level has risen on three successive measurements to 8.4%, and his leukocyte count has increased from 6,200/mm3 to 34,000/mm3. He reports taking the drug daily and has not started any new medications. A bone marrow examination shows 4% blasts and no additional cytogenetic abnormalities. Kinase domain mutation analysis identifies a T315I substitution. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Bosutinib
B. Dasatinib
C. Increase the imatinib dose
D. Nilotinib
E. Ponatinib
questions.explanation: T315I is the GATEKEEPER mutation. Threonine at position 315 forms a hydrogen bond that most tyrosine kinase inhibitors depend on for binding, and it also controls access to a hydrophobic pocket behind the ATP-binding site. Substituting the bulkier isoleucine removes that hydrogen bond and sterically blocks the pocket, so imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, and bosutinib ALL lose activity — this single substitution confers resistance across the entire first- and second-generation class. Ponatinib was designed around the problem: a carbon-carbon triple bond linker lets it thread past the bulky isoleucine, making it the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor with meaningful activity against T315I (asciminib, which binds an allosteric myristoyl pocket rather than the ATP site, is the other option). Ponatinib carries a serious arterial thrombotic and hepatotoxicity burden, so it is reserved for exactly this situation. The rising transcript level with confirmed adherence and no new interacting drugs is what should prompt mutation analysis in the first place; he remains in chronic phase, since 20% or more blasts would define blast phase and 20% or more basophils accelerated phase.

wrongExplanations.0: Bosutinib is a second-generation inhibitor active against many imatinib-resistant mutations, but T315I is specifically NOT among them. It fails for the same steric reason as the others.
wrongExplanations.1: Dasatinib is more potent than imatinib and covers a broad range of resistance mutations, which makes it the standard next step after most imatinib failures. T315I is the well-known exception that it does not cover.
wrongExplanations.2: Dose escalation is a reasonable strategy for suboptimal response WITHOUT a resistance mutation, or when adherence or a drug interaction is suspected. Here the target itself can no longer bind the drug, so no achievable concentration will restore activity.
wrongExplanations.3: Nilotinib is likewise a second-generation agent with broad mutational coverage and higher potency, and it is likewise inactive against T315I. Choosing any second-generation drug here is the central trap of the question.

questions.eli5: His leukemia drug works by slotting into a pocket on the abnormal protein driving the cancer. One letter of the protein changed to a bulkier one, and now the drug no longer fits — and neither do most of the alternatives. Only one drug was specifically engineered with a shape that can squeeze past that bulge.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease is admitted for a vaso-occlusive pain crisis involving both hips and the lower back. She is treated with intravenous fluids and patient-controlled intravenous hydromorphone, with good pain control by the evening of admission. On hospital day 2 she develops fever and pleuritic chest pain and becomes progressively dyspneic. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 85% on 6 L/min by nasal cannula. Auscultation shows decreased breath sounds with crackles over both lower lung fields. A chest x-ray, normal on admission, now shows new bilateral lower lobe opacities. Her hemoglobin concentration has fallen from 9.1 g/dL on admission to 6.4 g/dL, and her platelet count is 148,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Incentive spirometry and continued observation
B. Increase the hydromorphone infusion rate
C. Initiation of hydroxyurea
D. Red cell exchange transfusion
E. Transfusion of one unit of packed erythrocytes
questions.explanation: This is ACUTE CHEST SYNDROME — a new pulmonary infiltrate with fever and respiratory symptoms in a patient with sickle cell disease — and it is the leading cause of death in this population. The mechanism is a vicious cycle: opioids and splinting from rib and back pain cause hypoventilation and atelectasis, marrow fat and infection add insult, local hypoxia triggers further sickling within the pulmonary microvasculature, and that sickling worsens the hypoxia. Severity decides the transfusion strategy, and every marker here is severe: multilobar involvement, an oxygen saturation of 85% despite 6 L/min, and a hemoglobin that has fallen 2.7 g/dL. EXCHANGE transfusion is indicated because it does what simple transfusion cannot — it rapidly REMOVES sickled erythrocytes and drives the HbS fraction below roughly 30% without raising the hematocrit and worsening viscosity. Antibiotics covering atypical organisms, oxygen, incentive spirometry, and careful analgesia all continue alongside it.

wrongExplanations.0: Incentive spirometry is genuinely important — it prevents acute chest syndrome and is part of treatment — but as the sole management of a patient saturating 85% on 6 L/min with bilateral infiltrates and a falling hemoglobin, it is dangerously insufficient.
wrongExplanations.2: Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin, which interferes with HbS polymerization, and it reduces the FUTURE frequency of pain crises and acute chest episodes. Its effect takes weeks to months, so it does nothing for the current emergency — though it should absolutely be started before discharge.
wrongExplanations.1: Increasing the opioid dose is the actively harmful option and completes the vicious cycle: more opioid means more hypoventilation, more atelectasis, more hypoxia, and more sickling. Analgesia must be balanced against respiratory drive here, not simply escalated.
wrongExplanations.4: Simple transfusion is appropriate for MILD acute chest syndrome with modest hypoxia. In severe disease it raises the hematocrit and therefore viscosity without removing the sickled cells, so it dilutes rather than replaces the HbS burden and risks worsening microvascular occlusion.

questions.eli5: Pain medicine made her breathe shallowly, parts of her lungs collapsed, and low oxygen made her red cells sickle inside the lung vessels — which lowered oxygen further. Simply adding more blood would thicken it and make the jam worse. Exchanging her blood swaps the sickled cells out for normal ones without thickening it.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man comes to the office because of a 9-month history of fatigue and episodes of dark, cola-colored urine that are most noticeable on waking. Over the past week he has had progressive abdominal pain and distention. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, mild ascites, and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  8.6 g/dL
    Hematocrit                                  26%
    Leukocyte count                             2,800/mm3
    Platelet count                              88,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count                          6.2%
    Lactate dehydrogenase                       1,320 U/L
    Total bilirubin                             2.8 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin                            0.4 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)

A direct antiglobulin test is negative. Urinalysis shows hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria. Doppler ultrasonography shows thrombosis of the hepatic veins. Flow cytometry of peripheral erythrocytes and granulocytes shows absent CD55 and CD59. Treatment with eculizumab is planned. Which of the following is most important before this therapy is initiated?
choices: A. Human leukocyte antigen typing of potential sibling donors
B. Measurement of serum iron and ferritin
C. Screening for chronic hepatitis B infection
D. Testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation
E. Vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a clonal stem cell disorder in which a somatic PIGA mutation prevents synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor that tethers CD55 and CD59 to the cell surface. Both are complement regulators, so without them the patient's own complement lyses erythrocytes continuously — giving INTRAVASCULAR hemolysis with a negative antiglobulin test, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria, a very high lactate dehydrogenase, and an undetectable haptoglobin. The Budd-Chiari syndrome here is the classic thrombosis at an unusual site, and the pancytopenia reflects the underlying marrow failure. Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody against C5 that prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex — which is exactly why it is dangerous. Blocking terminal complement leaves the patient functionally deficient in the pathway that lyses NEISSERIA, and the risk of meningococcal disease rises roughly 1,000- to 2,000-fold. Meningococcal vaccination (conjugate ACWY and serogroup B) is required at least 2 weeks before the first dose, with antibiotic prophylaxis if therapy cannot be delayed, and the drug carries a boxed warning to that effect.

wrongExplanations.2: Hepatitis B screening is mandatory before RITUXIMAB and other B-cell-depleting or strongly immunosuppressive therapies, because of the risk of viral reactivation and fulminant hepatitis. Eculizumab does not deplete B cells and does not carry that reactivation risk.
wrongExplanations.3: JAK2 V617F testing is appropriate in the workup of an unexplained hepatic vein thrombosis, since a myeloproliferative neoplasm is the other major cause of Budd-Chiari syndrome. But his diagnosis has already been established by flow cytometry, and the result would not change the safety step needed before dosing.
wrongExplanations.1: Iron studies are genuinely relevant in this disease, because continuous urinary iron loss as hemosiderin makes these patients iron DEFICIENT despite ongoing hemolysis. That is a management point, not a safety prerequisite for starting complement blockade.
wrongExplanations.0: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is the only curative option and donor typing may become relevant, particularly given his marrow failure. It is not a prerequisite for beginning eculizumab and would not prevent the specific infection this drug predisposes to.

questions.eli5: His red blood cells are missing the shields that stop his own immune system's complement proteins from punching holes in them. The drug works by switching that whole complement pathway off — but that same pathway is what kills meningitis bacteria. So he must be vaccinated against them before the drug is started.
